title: The truth shall make you free (John 8:31–32)
word: The truth shall make you free
hookLine: freedom comes from continuing in his word

lines: A SENTENCE THAT STARTS WITH IF.
cards: Still in the temple, still the same long argument, and John points to some people in the crowd who have just come to believe in him. A teacher might greet new followers with a welcome.
Jesus gives them a sentence that starts with a condition: if. The second half is well-known on its own, and on its own it can sound like a slogan about facts.
Today, the whole sentence, and how fast these new believers start arguing about who is free.

teach.h: IF YOU CONTINUE IN MY WORD.
teach.b: Here's the whole sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "If you continue in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed. And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." It begins with if.
If you continue: stay, remain, keep living in my word. Freedom doesn't come at the start; it comes from staying. And truth here isn't first of all a fact you look up.

teach.h: TRUTH: A PERSON, NOT ONLY A FACT.
teach.b: In John's Gospel, truth is close to a person: later Jesus will say, I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Catholic readers hear knowing the truth as coming to know him, over time, by staying. His listeners bristle.
We are Abraham's children, they say, and we've never been slaves to anyone.
Jesus answers that he means another kind of slavery: "whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin." The thing you can't stop doing. The lie you have to keep up.
The habit that runs you. Then: if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed. Saint John Paul the Second's letter on moral life, The Splendor of Truth, keeps coming back to this verse.
Freedom, he wrote, isn't doing whatever we like; it depends on truth and grows by living in it. Every lie needs guarding.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.
teach.b: Every truth you finally tell is one less thing to guard.

how: Catholics hear John 8:31–42 at a weekday Mass in the fifth week of Lent, and the Church's moral teaching, especially Saint John Paul II's Veritatis Splendor, draws on it to link freedom with truth.

games.q: what does “the truth shall make you free” mean?
o: knowing enough facts frees you from all rules
staying in his word frees you from sin's hold
telling the truth keeps you out of a prison

games.q: the whole sentence — tap the pairs.
p: John Paul II on freedom and truth

s: the line begins: the truth shall make you free
it begins with if: if you continue in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed.
Jesus was speaking to people who had come to believe in him
in John's Gospel, truth is only a matter of facts
Jesus will later say: I am the way, and the truth, and the life.

games.q: you're telling new believers how to become truly free. what do you say comes first?
o: break every rule that binds you.
games.why: "If you continue in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed. And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."

practice: Let one small thing come to mind that you haven't said: I'm the one who broke it, I'm actually not fine, I liked your idea more than I said.
Notice how much effort it takes to keep it unsaid, and picture saying it, plainly and kindly. If you pray, ask for the courage to say it; if not, just hold it there a moment.

wordCard.voice: The truth shall make you free. Jesus's promise to those who continue in his word. In John, truth is close to a person. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: truth (John 8:32), a key word in John's Gospel; Jesus will say, I am the truth.

carryVoice: Your line: the truth sets free. Freedom grows by staying in his word. Until tomorrow.
